title: His ideal club and mix of styles
summary: He imagines a combo mixing ragtime, Dixieland and swing.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: Let's say this. Suppose that all commercial considerations were put aside, and you were given this club, and somebody would say, play anything you want, use whatever kind of a combo you want. What would you think would be the ideal kind of group you'd want to build? And what kind of music would you be playing?

I think if I was turned, if this club was turned over to me, and they'd say, now you put whatever you want in there, you play whatever you want, I think I would say, well, now maybe for one set, we're going to play a certain type of music, maybe 10 or 15 minutes of ragtime. And then maybe we'd come back the next set and say, well, now we're going to devote the next 15 minutes to some real good jazz. Or maybe we'll come back and play 15 minutes to something else. In other words, I don't think that I would particularly want to make it one particular type of music. I think it's good to play all types. Of course, it may be getting in a little bit of a commercial sort of a groove this way, but I think if you play good ragtime, Dixieland, even the good swing piano, the good swing era, maybe not just piano, but the swing era alone, you know, was a great era. And I think if you play all of this music and combine it and put it together, I mean, I think you've got some good music. And I don't think that it, I really believe that it can become tiresome listening to any particular one thing too long.
Right. Especially if you do have wider scope and you're not using your fullest abilities.

That's right. That's right. In other words, playing ragtime in Dixieland does not give you the full scope that you would really like to have. I mean, it doesn't give you the real full freedom of improvisation that you would like to have.
